---
title: "Density of Rational and Irrational Numbers"
categories: ["atomization"]
---

::: {.callout-note}
## Question

Given real numbers $a<b$, prove that the interval $(a,b)$ contains both a rational number and an irrational number. You may use the fact that $\sqrt2$ is irrational.
:::

## Rational Numbers Are Dense

The Archimedean property lets us choose a positive integer $n$ with $n(b-a)>1$. The interval $(na,nb)$ is then longer than $1$, so it contains an integer $m$. Divide $na<m<nb$ by $n$ to get
$$
a<\frac mn<b.
$$
Thus $r=m/n$ is a rational number in $(a,b)$.

## Irrational Numbers Are Dense

Choose the rational $r$ above. Because $b-r>0$, we can take a sufficiently large positive integer $N$ such that $\sqrt2/N<b-r$. Set
$$
s=r+\frac{\sqrt2}{N}.
$$
Then $a<r<s<b$. The number $s$ is irrational: otherwise $N(s-r)=\sqrt2$ would be rational, a contradiction. Hence every nonempty open interval contains an irrational number as well.
